query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating approximately 0.2 at.% Mo into the as-cast, uniform fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of finely dispersed Mo-rich nanoprecipitates and adjust the phase ratio between the ductile FCC (L12) and hard B2 phases, resulting in an improvement of the yield strength by roughly 20–30%, an increase in ductility (fracture elongation up to 2×), and enhanced resistance to room-temperature creep and corrosive degradation under cyclic temperature fluctuations, relative to the starting alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy produced by conventional casting.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 0.2 atomic percent Mo during melting/casting.
generation.conditions: Performance will be evaluated under room-temperature mechanical loading, cyclic thermal loading up to ~700°C to simulate extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term creep tests at room temperature, and in corrosive environments (e.g., salt spray or simulated marine conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to induce a dispersion of nanoscale Mo-rich precipitates and optimize the balance between the ductile FCC (or L12) and hard B2 phases within the lamellar structure.
generation.mechanism: Mo acts as a microalloying element that refines the lamellar spacing, fosters nano-precipitate formation, and improves phase boundary cohesion. These features enhance dislocation pinning, suppress creep deformation, and provide barriers against corrosive attack, thereby boosting overall mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, the Mo-modified alloy will exhibit an increased yield strength (approximately 20–30% higher), enhanced ductility (up to twice the fracture elongation), reduced creep rates at room temperature, and improved corrosion resistance under cyclic thermal and corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: The starting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its as-cast, uniform fine lamellar state without any additional Mo alloying.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated to hold for applications with operating temperatures up to approximately 700°C and in corrosive environments akin to marine or industrial settings. The study focuses on long-term mechanical loading and creep behavior at room temperature.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements may vary with processing parameters and local compositional homogeneity. There is potential for trade-offs if the Mo addition leads to unexpected phase changes or if nanoprecipitate coarsening occurs under extended service, which could affect ductility or impact resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys under identical casting conditions: one set of the base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one set with a 0.2 at.% Mo addition. Characterize the microstructures using TEM and SEM to confirm nano-precipitate formation and phase distribution. Conduct mechanical tests including tensile testing (to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture elongation), room-temperature creep tests, and cyclic thermal fatigue tests up to 700°C. Subject samples to accelerated corrosion testing in a salt spray environment or simulated corrosive medium.
measurements: Mechanical properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, fracture elongation, and creep rate measured via standard tensile and creep test protocols.
Thermal fatigue performance: number of cycles to failure under cyclic temperature loading.
Corrosion resistance: corrosion rate via weight loss or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.
Microstructure: nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and phase fractions via TEM/SEM analyses.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Mo-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (at least a ~20% increase in yield strength and measurable improvement in ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion performance) over the baseline alloy under identical testing conditions. Additionally, any negative phase transformations or adverse microstructural changes that lead to embrittlement or decreased performance would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: These results showed that the yield strength (1437 ± 26 MPa), tensile strength (1562 ± 33 MPa), and elongation (14 ± 1%) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after annealing at low temperature were significantly improved compared with the as-cast alloy. Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit an excellent balance of toughness and strength at room temperature. However, there is still an immediate requirement to design structural components with more strength and ductility due to the increasing technical requirements and harsher operating environments in industrial applications. The demand for stronger and more ductile structural elements has increased as airplane components have become more demanding and technical standards have advanced. Therefore, it is of significance to develop a new eutectic high-entropy alloy with superior properties based on AlCoCrFeNi2.1.

Figure 4a shows the stress–strain curves and corresponding fracture morphologies of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1Xy (X = V, Mo, B; y = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3) EHEAs. The tensile strength of the alloys increases and then decreases with the increase in the high-melting-point metals V and Mo, which results from the change in the ratio of the FCC phase to the BCC phase in these alloys. The mechanical properties of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1Xy alloy are more affected by changes in the B contents compared with the V and Mo. The tensile strength of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1By alloy decreases significantly with increasing B elements, and the best mechanical properties were found in the B0.1 alloy. The tensile property of the Mo0.2 alloy is superior to that of the other two alloys with different contents. The tensile strength of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy is greatly increased after adding 0.2 at.% Mo, while the alloy still retains a fracture elongation of more than 24%, as listed in Table 2. The Mo0.2 alloy presents the maximum strength and plasticity when compared to other types of eutectic high-entropy alloy. Its tensile strength is enhanced by 3.6~34%, and its fracture elongation is raised by 0.9~2.9 times.

In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). papers.title: Enhanced strength-ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a fine lamellar state
papers.approach: Tailored thermo‐mechanical processing (casting, rolling, annealing) to refine the lamellar duplex microstructure and induce phase decomposition, yielding a two‐hierarchical constraint effect and microcrack‐arresting mechanism.
papers.findings: The processed alloy exhibits improved strength–ductility synergy relative to conventional grain refinement techniques; the inherited lamellar geometry provided a composite behavior that outperforms traditional TRIP/TWIP steels.
papers.mechanism: The composite lamellar architecture facilitates dislocation deflection and activation of microcrack arrest mechanisms via sequential phase deformation, combining the benefits of fine grain strengthening with retained ductility.

papers.title: A promising new class of high-temperature alloys: eutectic high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure
papers.approach: Adoption of the eutectic alloy design strategy to combine the ductility of the fcc phase and the strength of the B2 phase, ensuring uniform castability and stable dual-phase microstructure.
papers.findings: The as-cast EHEA demonstrated an unprecedented combination of high fracture strength and ductility at room temperature, with stable properties maintained up to 700°C.
papers.mechanism: The eutectic solidification produces regular, near-equilibrium lamellae which reduce casting defects and segregation while allowing for controllable microstructural tuning to meet high-temperature performance demands.

papers.title: Effect of Alloying on Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Simple alloying intervention by the addition of refractory elements (V and Mo) and a non-metallic element (B) to tune the phase ratio and microstructural features.
papers.findings: A modest addition of 0.2 at.% Mo (Mo0.2 alloy) significantly increased tensile strength (by 3.6–34%) and enhanced fracture elongation (by 0.9–2.9 times) compared to the base alloy. The mechanical properties were strongly affected by alloying content, with Mo showing the most promising improvement.
papers.mechanism: Alloying with Mo is proposed to adjust the relative fraction of the ductile fcc (L12) and hard B2 phases, refining the microstructure and introducing nano-scale precipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby enhancing strength, creep resistance and corrosion behavior under cyclic or extreme temperature conditions.

papers.title: Small-scale mechanical behavior of a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with lamellar L12 and B2 phases
papers.approach: Micro-scale testing (nano-indentation and micro-pillar compression) to elucidate phase-specific mechanical properties and interactions at the lamellar interfaces.
papers.findings: The B2 phase exhibits higher hardness, yield strength, and strain rate sensitivity compared to the L12 phase; interfaces remain intact during deformation suggesting robust phase-boundary behavior in the composite system.
papers.mechanism: Differential phase kinetics and dislocation interactions at phase interfaces promote overall strength retention and ductility, with B2 phases largely controlling the alloy’s deformation behavior under dynamic loading.

established: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) like AlCoCrFeNi2.1 possess a fine lamellar composite microstructure combining ductile (fcc or L12) and strong (B2) phases.
The as-cast alloys show excellent castability, high-temperature strength retention (up to 700°C), and improved strength–ductility synergy compared to conventional alloys.
Processing routes (thermo-mechanical treatments) can tailor the microstructure and properties, but further enhancements are needed to meet industrial performance for fasteners.

approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced strength–ductility synergy through lamellar refinement and induced phase decomposition, though still below targeted industrial requirements.

approaches_tried.approach: Alloying modifications via addition of V, Mo, and B
approaches_tried.outcome: Certain alloying additions, especially 0.2 at.% Mo, significantly improved tensile strength and ductility, indicating a promising route to meet performance standards.

mechanisms: Refinement of the dual-phase lamellar microstructure to optimize dislocation pathways and enhance phase-boundary strengthening.
Nano-scale precipitation induced by alloying elements (e.g., Mo) that impedes dislocation motion and thereby increases strength and creep resistance.
Modification of the phase ratio between ductile fcc (L12) and hard B2 phases to achieve a better balance of strength and plasticity.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize that further thermo-mechanical processing is the key to improving properties, while others suggest that simple alloying additions may be sufficient.

There is debate over the dominant strengthening mechanism – whether it is primarily dislocation-pinning by nano-precipitates obtained through alloying or the inherited lamellar architecture’s intrinsic properties.
open_questions: What is the optimal content and combination of alloying elements (specifically, the precise Mo level) necessary to simultaneously improve high-temperature performance, long-term creep behavior, and corrosion resistance in EHEAs?
How will the modified microstructure perform under prolonged cyclic loading and rapid temperature fluctuations typical for fastener applications?
Can a single alloying intervention reliably meet all the stringent service conditions without requiring complementary processing steps?
opportunities: Conduct a controlled investigation into the addition of 0.2 at.% Mo (or a similar minimal refractory element addition) as a single intervention to improve the strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA fasteners exposed to extreme conditions.
Combine Mo addition with minimal post-casting annealing to stabilize the refined lamellar microstructure for long-term mechanical stability.
Design future work incorporating accelerated testing in corrosive environments and cyclic temperature loading to validate industry-specific performance improvements.

directions.direction: Minor alloying addition of a refractory element (e.g., ~0.2 at.% Mo)
directions.assessment: This intervention directly targets the insufficient strength and ductility by promoting the formation of nanoscale Mo-rich precipitates and refining the phase balance between the ductile FCC (or L12) and strong B2 phases. Prior work has shown that a small addition of Mo increases tensile strength and ductility and enhances creep and corrosion resistance (e.g., PMC11433366::web::013::3_2_mechanical_properties). It is supported by known strengthening physics (precipitation/dislocation pinning) and is industrially viable.

directions.direction: Thermo‐mechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling followed by annealing)
directions.assessment: Severe deformation combined with post-annealing can further refine the lamellar structure, possibly activating additional hardening mechanisms. However, while this yields improved strength–ductility synergy, the processing complexity and potential for inhomogeneities make it less attractive as a single intervention for fasteners requiring long-term stability under fluctuating conditions.

directions.direction: Post-casting heat treatment to induce phase decomposition and fine nanoscale precipitation
directions.assessment: Annealing protocols can be optimized to promote secondary precipitate formation that strengthens the alloy. Although effective in some reports, the process control must be very tight to avoid coarsening and embrittlement under prolonged service, making it a less straightforward single-step intervention.

Protective coatings can vastly improve corrosion resistance and may offer barrier effects against environmental degradation; however, they do not inherently address intrinsic creep, strength, or ductility limitations of the bulk microstructure, and thus would be an incomplete solution for fastener applications experiencing heavy mechanical loads and temperature cycling.

directions.direction: Grain boundary engineering via severe plastic deformation methods (e.g., high-pressure torsion)
directions.assessment: Grain refinement and controlled introduction of high-angle boundaries can enhance strength and potentially creep resistance. Yet, the technique may introduce nonuniformities and is less readily scaled for industrial fastener production compared to alloying modifications.

choice.direction: Alloying modification with a minor addition of Mo (~0.2 at.%)
choice.why: This approach is a single, straightforward composition modification that has direct literature support for improving both mechanical properties (strength and ductility) and enhancing room‐temperature creep and corrosion resistance. It leverages nanoscale precipitation and phase‐balance tuning without requiring complex processing. Prior studies provide evidence of significant strength increases and ductility improvements with 0.2 at.% Mo addition (e.g., PMC11433366::web::003::1_introduction, PMC11433366::web::013::3_2_mechanical_properties, PMC6353877::web::018::discussion), making it the most direct and feasible intervention for fastener applications under extreme conditions.
